content: Pubic hair refers to the hair that grows in the frontal genital region, the crotch, and sometimes at the upper inner thighs. These areas collectively form what is known as the pubic region. During childhood, this area is covered with fine vellus hair. However, the term pubic hair is typically used to describe the coarser, longer hair that develops during puberty as a result of increasing androgen levels. Pubic hair is classified as androgenic hair. Development of Pubic Hair Before puberty, both boys and girls have very fine vellus hair in the genital area, which is referred to as Tanner stage 1 hair. As puberty begins, the body produces increasing levels of sex hormones known as androgens. In response, the skin in the genital area starts to grow thicker, often curlier hair with a faster growth rate. The onset of pubic hair development is termed pubarche. While the transformation of individual hair follicles is relatively abrupt, the area of skin that grows androgenic hair expands gradually over several years. In most females, pubic hair first appears along the edges of the labia majora (Tanner stage 2) and spreads forward to the mons pubis (Tanner stage 3) over the next two years. By 2–3 years into puberty, which is approximately the time of menarche for most girls, the pubic triangle becomes densely filled with hair. Within another two years, pubic hair also begins to grow on the upper thighs in most young women and, in some cases, extends slightly upward along the midline of the abdomen toward the umbilicus. In males, the first pubic hair appears as a few sparse hairs on the scrotum or at the upper base of the penis (Tanner stage 2). Within a year, the hair around the base of the penis becomes too numerous to count (Tanner stage 3). Over the next 3–4 years, the hair fills the pubic area (Tanner stage 4), becoming much thicker and darker. By five years into puberty, pubic hair extends to the upper thighs and upward along the abdomen toward the umbilicus (Tanner stage 5). Other areas of the skin are also sensitive to androgens, though slightly less so, and androgenic hair typically appears in these regions somewhat later. In order of sensitivity to androgens and the appearance of androgenic hair, these areas include the armpits (axillae), perianal region, upper lip, preauricular areas (sideburns), periareolar areas (nipples), the middle of the chest, the neck under the chin, the remainder of the chest and beard area, limbs and shoulders, back, and buttocks. Although pubarche is generally considered part of the process of puberty, it is distinct and independent from the maturation of the gonads, which leads to sexual maturation and fertility. Pubic hair can develop solely from adrenal androgens and may appear even in cases where the ovaries or testes are defective and nonfunctional. Differences in Hair Growth Between Sexes There is little, if any, difference in the capacity of male and female bodies to grow hair in response to androgens. The noticeable sex-dimorphic differences in hair distribution between men and women are primarily due to differences in androgen levels reached during maturity. Patterns of pubic hair growth vary widely. In some individuals, pubic hair is thick and coarse, while in others, it may be sparse and fine. Hair texture can range from tightly curled to completely straight. These patterns can also vary by race and ethnicity. Characteristics of Pubic Hair Pubic hair and axillary (armpit) hair can differ significantly in color from scalp hair. In most people, pubic hair is darker, although it can also be lighter. On most women, the pubic patch is triangular and lies over the mons veneris, or mound of Venus. On many men, the pubic patch tapers upward into a line of hair pointing toward the navel, forming a roughly upward-pointing triangle. As with axillary hair, pubic hair is associated with a concentration of sebaceous glands in the area.
